title: IRS Form 56: How Executors Notify the IRS (November 2026)
summary: This November 2026 overview explains IRS Form 56 filing for executors, including fiduciary relationships and termination requirements.
body_markdown:
During estate settlement, an executor or administrator notifies the IRS of their role by filing Form 56, the Notice Concerning Fiduciary Relationship. The form reports authority the executor already holds through a court appointment or legal document. The form does not grant that authority. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: who files Form 56, when the notice is filed, how each part is completed, which documents support the notice, where the form is mailed, how Form 56 differs from Form 2848, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Form 56 notifies the IRS of an executor's authority; it does not grant that authority.
- Executors generally file Form 56 promptly after gaining legal authority.
- Form 56 is mailed to the taxpayer's IRS service center. Online filing is unavailable.
- Another Form 56 reports when the executor's role ends, separate from the final tax return.


## What Is IRS Form 56?


IRS Form 56, titled “Notice Concerning Fiduciary Relationship,” notifies the IRS that someone has legal authority to handle tax matters for another person or estate, including an executor acting for an estate.


The IRS Form 56 overview explains that the form reports the creation or termination of a fiduciary relationship. Filing provides notice; the executor’s authority comes from the legal appointment, not the form.


{{blog-cta-financial}}


## What Is a Fiduciary Relationship?


A fiduciary relationship exists when someone acts in a position of trust on behalf of another person or entity. The[IRS Form 56 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i56) include executors, administrators, trustees, guardians, and receivers within that definition.


An executor or administrator is a fiduciary because they act on the estate’s behalf. Families often encounter the term during estate settlement, but Form 56 applies beyond estates.


## Who Must File Form 56?


Executors and administrators handling an estate’s federal tax matters must notify the IRS of their fiduciary role. Form 56 provides that notice. Trustees, guardians, and conservators acting for a taxpayer have the same obligation.


The notice requirement applies when the fiduciary relationship begins. Being named executor in a will does not, by itself, trigger filing before the person has authority to act, which generally requires[letters of administration](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-get-letters-of-administration) or similar court appointment for an administrator.


## When Form 56 Should Be Filed


Form 56 is generally filed promptly after an executor gains authority, before or alongside the relevant income tax return:


- The person’s final income tax return (Form 1040).
- The estate’s income tax return,[Form 1041](https://www.elayne.com/resources/form-1041-estate-tax-return) .


This tells the IRS who handles tax matters.


When the fiduciary role ends, another Form 56, with Part II completed as applicable, reports termination separately from the estate’s final tax return.


## Form 56 vs. Form 2848


Form 56 notifies the IRS of an existing fiduciary role; Form 2848 appoints a tax representative.


Form Purpose


Form 56 Reports authority arising under law or court appointment.


Form 2848 Authorizes an eligible representative, such as an attorney or CPA, to act before the IRS.


The[IRS power of attorney instructions](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2848.pdf) explain the distinction.


## How to Complete Form 56: Part-by-Part Walkthrough


The Form 56 instructions explain these fields:


- Part I identifies the taxpayer and fiduciary, including tax IDs and contact details.
- Section A records authority, such as court appointment or a trust instrument.
- Section B lists tax liabilities, returns, and periods, which ties into how executors[track tax returns and filing statuses](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-track-all-tax-returns-and-filing-statuses-during-estate-administration) throughout administration.
- Part IV requires signature, title, and date.


- Line 1f includes receiver and fiduciary.
- Lines 2c and 2d cover appointments and court control or custody of all or substantially all taxpayer assets.


These entries describe the fiduciary's role and the basis for acting on the taxpayer's behalf.


## Part II: Revoking or Terminating the Fiduciary Notice


Part II of IRS Form 56 reports changes to previously reported fiduciary authority:


- Section A covers total revocation or termination, such as when an executor’s authority ends.
- Section B covers partial revocation, identifying tax matters or periods excluded from the earlier notice.
- Section C names a substitute fiduciary, such as a successor trustee.


For a departing co-executor, the notice identifies whose authority ended and any replacement.


## Part III: Court and Administrative Proceedings


Part III of IRS Form 56 records court and administrative proceedings connected to the fiduciary relationship. For an estate in formal probate, court paperwork provides the case details:


- The court’s name and location.
- The proceeding’s docket number and type.
- The date the proceeding began.
- The date, time, and place of any applicable hearing.


These entries connect the fiduciary relationship to the estate’s court case, and the specific documentation required can vary by jurisdiction.


## What Documents to Attach


Supporting documents for IRS Form 56 depend on the fiduciary relationship selected in Section A. Evidence of authority may need to be attached or referenced:


- [Letters testamentary](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-get-letters-testamentary-new-york) for a court-appointed executor.
- Letters of administration for an administrator.
- A trust instrument and amendments for a trustee.


The Form 56 instructions explain what accompanies the notice.


## Where to File Form 56


IRS Form 56 must be mailed; online submission is unavailable.


Under the[IRS mailing location rules](https://www.irs.gov/filing/where-to-file-forms-beginning-with-the-number-5) , executors send it to the service center where the taxpayer files returns. For a final Form 1040, the taxpayer’s state determines the center.


The[2026 fiduciary filing clarification](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/clarified-filing-addresses-for-fiduciaries) reserves the separate Dallas insolvency destination for receivers, similar fiduciaries, and assignees for creditors’ benefit, not ordinary executors.

## How Elayne Supports Executors Through the Tax and Settlement Process


Elayne is an online service that works through an estate with families, one step at a time: getting legal authority, finding what the person owned and owed, and handling the estate account through the final accounting.


Authority to act for an estate comes from the court, not from a tax form. The court documents that authority as letters testamentary for an executor named in a will, or letters of administration for an administrator when there is no will. Form 56 then notifies the IRS of the role the court has already given. Elayne keeps the court paperwork and estate details in one place, so the information that tax forms such as Form 56 ask for stays organized.


Elayne holds IRS authorization to request a person's IRS tax transcripts, which cover 10 years. A tax transcript is not a tax return. A transcript is a record of what banks, brokerages, employers, and insurers reported to the IRS about the person.


Elayne also requests the person's Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, cards, and debts in the person's name. Elayne checks more than 100 other sources as well. Each finding is added to the estate inventory with the source of the information.


The transcripts also show whether the estate owes the IRS a balance or is owed a refund. Debts appear alongside assets, so the estate's obligations are visible before any money is paid out. An Estate Expert from Elayne's team reviews the findings with the family in a one-on-one call.


Once the court has appointed an executor or administrator, Elayne works through each bank and company with that person, one account at a time. Each institution has its own forms and process for releasing an account, and Elayne tracks what each one needs. Elayne obtains the estate's tax ID (EIN), helps open the estate account in the estate's name, and records every deposit and payment.


The estate account is connected, so the family's attorney can see its activity without needing a bank login. The final accounting is then handed to the executor and the family's attorney.


The executor remains responsible for the estate's tax filings, including Form 1041, which a CPA or other tax professional typically prepares. The attorney advises on legal questions, and the executor decides how the estate is administered. Elayne provides the estate inventory and account history that the CPA and attorney work from. The executor and the family's attorney close the estate.


Elayne is an eligible estate expense: the cost can be paid from the estate account or reimbursed by the estate. Before the estate account is open, the Estate Setup fee is paid by the family and tracked with a receipt, and the estate can repay that amount once the account opens.


## FAQ


### Does a fiduciary need separate IRS Forms 56 for the person who died and their estate?


Yes, if the fiduciary acts for both, separate Forms 56 are required because the person and the estate are separate taxpayers. The notice for the person uses their Social Security number; the estate’s notice uses its employer identification number (EIN).


### Can co-executors file one IRS Form 56 for both?


No. Each co-executor must file a separate IRS Form 56 to notify the IRS of their fiduciary relationship. Keeping copies of both notices with the estate’s tax records helps document who reported authority and which tax matters each notice covers.


### Where is the IRS Form 56 PDF available?


The[IRS Form 56 page](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-56) provides free links to the form and instructions.


### Which line applies when no court has appointed an administrator?


Line 1d applies to the fiduciary of a person who died without a valid will when no court-appointed administrator or representative exists. The instructions limit that box to the sole person charged with the property of the person who died. The date of death is entered on line 2a.
